Peter looked up, ashamed to be caught crying. He said his name grandly, as if names could repair shadows. Wendy offered to sew it back on.

"Will it hurt?" Peter asked, trying to sound as if pain were a subject he had never needed to consider. "I shall be careful," Wendy promised. "Then I shall not cry," he said, though his wet face suggested that this was a new decision.
She fetched her needle, and Peter held still with great difficulty. When she finished, he sprang up and danced around the room. "Look what I can do!" he cried.

He seemed to have forgotten that Wendy had done most of the work. She turned toward the wall, hurt by his careless pride. Peter noticed that something had gone wrong, though understanding feelings was harder for him than flying.

He coaxed her back into the conversation and gave her a little acorn button. She hung it on a chain, close to her heart. Peter told her about Neverland, where the Lost Boys waited for him beneath the trees.

They knew how to hunt, hide, and fight pirates, but nobody knew how to finish a bedtime story. Wendy could scarcely believe such a serious problem existed. "You could tell us stories," Peter suggested.

Tinker Bell rang furiously inside the drawer where he had accidentally shut her. He let her out, but her angry little light stayed close to Wendy's face. Wendy looked at her sleeping brothers, then at the wide night beyond the window.
An ordinary bedroom had suddenly become the edge of an extraordinary world.
Chapter 2: Above the Sleeping World. Wendy wanted to go, but an adventure was no excuse for leaving John and Michael behind. She shook them awake, and John put on his hat immediately.
He felt that a gentleman ought to be properly dressed when leaving by a window. Michael asked whether they would be back before breakfast. Peter had very little interest in breakfast times.

First, he explained, they must think of something wonderfully happy. The children tried, jumped from their beds, and landed on the floor with three heavy bumps. Peter laughed until Wendy asked whether he had forgotten anything.
He had forgotten the fairy dust. "You might have mentioned that," John said, rubbing his elbow. "I am mentioning it now," Peter replied cheerfully.

Wendy decided that arguing with him would use up the entire night. Once he sprinkled it over them, their feet began behaving like balloons. Michael floated toward the ceiling and discovered that coming down was not as easy as going up.
John attempted a careful turn and flew straight into a curtain. Wendy reached for the bedpost, frightened by the beautiful impossibility of it all. Then she let go.

They sailed through the window into the cool London air. Below them, street lamps stretched into shining lines, and roofs fitted together like pieces of a dark puzzle. Nana barked from the garden, pulling at the chain that kept her there.
For a moment Wendy wanted to turn back and explain everything. But Peter was already ahead, and the city was falling away behind them. They flew over fields, rivers, and the black shape of the sea.
Peter pointed into the sky and gave directions that sounded easier to say than to follow. Stars did not look much like street corners. John tried asking how far they had to go.

Peter gave an answer, changed it, and then decided that distance was not an interesting subject. Sometimes he flew away to inspect something, forgetting that his new companions could not manage quite so well. When Michael grew sleepy, he began to sink.
Peter swept down after him, catching him just before the ocean could. To Peter, it was a splendid game. To Wendy, it was a reminder that excitement and safety were not always close friends.

At last an island rose out of the blue distance. Its forests, mountains, and shining water felt strangely familiar, like the shape of a place remembered from dreams. Here were the paths they had imagined while lying in bed.
Here, too, were dangers that had seemed much smaller in those dreams. Peter's voice changed as he looked down. He pointed out the pirates' ship and warned them to fly quietly.
The pirates were watching the sky. A sudden shot split the air, scattering the children. Wendy lost sight of her brothers in the smoke and noise.

She followed Tinker Bell's bright light toward the forest, grateful for a guide. But the fairy had become fierce with jealousy. Below them, the Lost Boys looked up and saw a white figure moving between the branches.
Tinker Bell rang out a message, pretending it was Peter's order. The boys reached for their bows. Wendy, still thinking she had found help, began to come down.
An arrow flew toward her.
Chapter 3: The Little House in the Woods. Tootles was the boy who shot the arrow. He was usually the one who missed the most exciting adventures.
This time, he thought, he would have something important to tell Peter. Then Wendy fell, and the boys gathered around her in terrible silence. She was not a bird after all.

She was a girl, and the discovery made their proud little victory turn cold. Peter arrived carrying a promise of wonderful news. He had brought them a storyteller, perhaps even someone who would care for them like a mother.
Tootles looked from Peter to the still figure on the ground. "I shot her," he said. He did not run away or try to blame another boy.
Peter's face hardened, and he raised a weapon in anger. Then Wendy's hand moved. The arrow had struck the acorn button hanging on her chain, instead of entering her chest.
The little gift had saved her life. Peter put down his weapon, and the boys breathed again. Tinker Bell's secret did not stay hidden for long.

Peter banished her for what she had done, though Wendy, even while weak, asked him to soften the punishment. Forgiveness came more easily to Wendy than to the fairy who had hurt her. Now the boys faced another problem.
They had a girl lying in the forest, and waking her seemed terribly rude. It was decided that they should build a house around her. The plan suited Neverland perfectly.

The boys ran for branches, leaves, and everything else that might persuade a house to exist. Peter directed the work with the confidence of someone who had never paid a builder. When Wendy opened her eyes, a small doorway waited before her.
A roof of leaves stood above her, and the boys were trying to look like respectful visitors. They asked her to be their mother. Wendy reminded them that she was only a little girl.
They said that this was much better than having no mother at all. It was difficult to refuse people who made such hopeful faces. "You must promise to listen," she said.

The boys promised at once, which was easy because they had not yet discovered how much listening might be required. John and Michael soon arrived, dusty, excited, and full of questions about the arrows.

They were pleased to find Wendy alive, but less pleased to discover that she had become everybody's mother while they were away. Peter showed them the way to the underground home. Each boy had his own hollow tree, with a passage narrow enough to fit his body.

A person who ate too much might find getting home a serious problem. Wendy looked at the dark opening and imagined herself stuck halfway down, with dinner waiting below. The boys assured her that they could make a door especially for her.

Inside, a fire glowed, rough beds lined the walls, and the island's busy noises sounded far away. Wendy felt the first warm pleasure of being needed. She did not yet know how much work everybody's mother would have to do.
Above the roof of earth, pirates moved between the trees.

Chapter 4: Days That Felt Like Dreams. Life under the ground soon became a mixture of adventure and housework. Wendy discovered holes in clothes, missing buttons, and boys who believed washing was a punishment invented elsewhere.

She washed, mended, cooked, and tried to remember which child had last had a proper bath. Peter acted as the father of their pretend family whenever the idea amused him. At other times he disappeared into the forest, returning with a story nobody could entirely check.

It was not always clear whether his adventures had happened or whether he had simply decided they ought to have happened. In Neverland, the difference sometimes seemed unusually small. The children held meals at the underground table.

When there was real food, they ate real food. When Peter preferred pretending, everyone had to pretend with him, and hungry stomachs were expected to be good sports. "May I have another helping?" John asked once, holding out his empty plate.

"You have had three already," Peter told him. John looked at Wendy, hoping that somewhere in the family there was a person who understood the difference between a meal and an idea. John liked making rules for games.

Michael liked changing them just before he lost. The Lost Boys argued about turns, places, and whose story Wendy should tell next. She could stop a quarrel more easily with the promise of a story than with a command.

At bedtime, they pressed close to hear her voice. The fire made shadows climb the walls, and for a little while even Peter sat quietly. Wendy told them about a family in London with a dog for a nurse.
Michael listened as if the dog were an interesting invention. That troubled her. She began asking John and Michael questions about home.

What did their father look like, and where did their mother sit in the evening? John answered confidently, then paused when she asked for details. Michael remembered some things beautifully and other things not at all.

Wendy turned remembering into a kind of lesson, afraid that a place might vanish from their hearts if they stopped visiting it in their thoughts. Outside, the island offered a different lesson each day. They followed animal tracks through the wood, listened for footsteps, and learned which silences meant somebody was hiding.

Sometimes they saw mermaids lying in the sunlight by the lagoon. Wendy wished the mermaids would speak kindly to her, but they had no desire to welcome another girl. They laughed and splashed, showing bright tails before sliding away.

The children played near the water until its pleasant surface began to darken. Neverland was not equally friendly at every hour. As evening came, the lagoon seemed to keep secrets beneath its smooth skin.
Wendy noticed that Peter listened more carefully there. He might forget meals, promises, and the names of old friends. But he could hear danger moving in a place that looked empty.
One afternoon, while the others rested by the water, he lifted his head. A boat was approaching. It carried pirates and a prisoner who was trying very hard not to show fear.
Peter's smile sharpened. For him, the day had finally become interesting.

Chapter 5: The Captain Who Heard a Clock. Captain Hook had a fine coat, careful manners, and a metal hook where one hand should have been. He used the hook so easily that the pirates often forgot how frightening it looked to newcomers.

They never forgot for long. Hook could speak softly while planning something cruel, which made his softness unpleasant rather than comforting. He commanded his ship as if every rope and sailor owed him obedience.

Yet there was one sound that could turn this proud captain pale. Long ago, Peter had cut off his hand and thrown it to a crocodile. The animal enjoyed the meal and followed Hook, hoping for the rest of him.
It had also swallowed a clock. Whenever Hook heard ticking nearby, he knew its great jaws were coming closer. The pirates could see him listening even when he pretended not to be afraid.

Smee, who wore spectacles and looked less dangerous than he was, tried to comfort him. If the clock ever stopped, he pointed out, the crocodile might approach without a warning. This was not the sort of comfort Hook wanted.
"Do you think that makes the matter better?" the captain asked. Smee considered the question and began polishing his spectacles. It was safer to clean something than to answer too quickly.

What troubled the captain almost as much as the crocodile was Peter himself. Peter had no interest in behaving like a proper enemy. He laughed, flew, and treated Hook's serious plans as invitations to a game.

The captain wanted to defeat him, but he also wanted to understand what made the boy so impossible to shame. He thought about manners, dignity, and the correct appearance of a gentleman. Peter mostly thought about the next exciting thing.

Between them stood a quarrel neither of them could put down. Now Hook's pirates had captured Tiger Lily, the daughter of the island people's chief. They brought her to a rock in the lagoon where the rising water would soon reach her.
She stood bound and silent, refusing to beg. Hidden nearby, Wendy watched with Peter. The game had become something much more serious.
Peter could imitate voices wonderfully well. From his hiding place, he spoke in Hook's own tone and ordered the men to release their prisoner. The pirates stopped, confused.

They thought their captain had changed his mind, and obeying seemed safer than asking why. Tiger Lily slipped away before they discovered the trick. Then the real Hook appeared, and the lagoon filled with angry voices.

Peter answered from the shadows, enjoying the captain's confusion. Hook looked around, unable to tell whether the voice belonged to a boy, a spirit, or his own fear. The Lost Boys attacked the pirates, and the quiet water broke into splashes and shouts.
Wendy tried to find Peter among the moving figures. Above the fighting, the sunlight faded. Below it, the tide kept rising, with no interest in who won.
Chapter 6: The Rock and the Rising Tide. Peter and Hook met on a slippery rock, close enough for Peter to see the captain's anger in his eyes. Peter noticed that Hook stood lower than he did.
He offered him a hand to bring him up, because fighting from unequal positions did not seem fair. Hook answered by biting the offered hand. For a moment Peter was more astonished than hurt.
He had expected an enemy to fight, but the unfairness of the bite shocked him. The pause gave Hook a chance to strike again. Peter was wounded, and Wendy hurried toward him through the confusion.
Then the familiar ticking reached the captain's ears. His face changed at once. He fled, abandoning the fight, as the crocodile moved through the darkening water.
The other children escaped with the boat, believing Wendy and Peter would follow. Instead, the two were left on the rock. Water climbed around their feet.

Peter tried to fly, but he was too weak to carry Wendy, and the rising tide gave them little time. Wendy looked at the space between the rock and the shore. It had seemed a short distance in the afternoon.
Now it looked like a different country. A kite drifted toward them, tugging at a loose string. Peter caught it and tied the string around Wendy.
It could carry one person to safety, he said. Wendy wanted him to come too. "We could hold on together," she said.

Peter tested the pull of the string and shook his head. "It would not carry us both," he answered, and for once there was no room in his voice for pretending. He shook his head and sent her away before she could keep arguing.
The wind lifted her above the water, taking her toward the waiting boys. Peter remained alone. The rock became smaller and smaller beneath him.

For once, there was nobody to admire his courage and nobody to laugh at his jokes. He tried to meet the danger as another adventure, but even the bravest words could not lower the sea. Then a bird came toward him, pushing a nest across the water.
Her eggs lay inside it. The nest had been washed away, and she had spent a long time trying to keep it safe. Now she was offering it to the boy.
Peter and the bird could not understand each other's speech. She shouted in bird language; he replied with great confidence in his own. Both thought the other was behaving rather foolishly.
At last he understood the important part without understanding a single word. The nest could hold him. He would not leave her eggs in the water, so he moved them into a floating hat.
The bird settled on the hat, and Peter climbed into the nest. They floated away, two small boats sharing the same escape. When Peter returned to the underground home, Wendy threw her arms around him.

The boys cheered and demanded every detail. Peter enjoyed telling it, but the nest in the dark had taught him something his proud voice did not quite explain. For a little while, his life had depended on an ordinary bird deciding to help.
Chapter 7: A Story That Led Home. After Peter saved Tiger Lily, her people helped guard the underground home. The children felt safer, and the days continued in their bright, untidy fashion.

Wendy still had washing to do, even when everybody else had been fighting pirates. She wondered whether mothers ever received a day off after an adventure. One evening, she gathered the boys around the fire and began a familiar story.

There had once been three children, she told them, who flew away from their parents. Their mother had loved them, and their father had loved them too, although fathers sometimes showed it badly. The children visited a wonderful island and stayed away for a long time.
At first they remembered every part of home. Then the smaller memories began to fade. Wendy paused, watching John and Michael.

Michael leaned against her, listening with the calm of a child who expected the world to look after him. In her story, the mother kept a window open, waiting for the children to return. Wendy said this with absolute confidence.
Whatever happened, surely the window would still be open. Peter interrupted. He said mothers did not always wait.
He had once gone back to his own window, he explained, and found it closed. Another child had taken his place. His voice was hard and casual, but the room seemed colder after he spoke.
Wendy could not tell how much he remembered clearly and how much belonged to his hurt. She could hear that something in the memory frightened him. And suddenly it frightened her too.

What if her mother was waiting now, while she sat beneath another island telling stories? What if loving someone meant going back before waiting became endless? She stood and began finding her brothers' things.
They must leave for London at once. John agreed, though he wished the decision had been made on a day with less promising weather for adventure. Michael asked whether their mother would know them.
That question made Wendy pack faster. The Lost Boys watched her in dismay. They asked who would tell stories and remember their bedtime rules.
Wendy invited them to come too. Perhaps her parents could find room for children who had no home waiting for them. The boys began gathering their belongings with sudden hope.
Peter laughed too loudly and said he was glad to have fewer people crowding the place. Wendy knew that laughter could hide more than amusement. She asked him to come with them.
He refused at once. "You would not have to be grown-up straight away," Wendy said. "I would have to begin," Peter answered.

She could not deny it, and he looked almost pleased to have found the part of her promise that frightened him. Going home meant growing up, and Peter would not agree to either. Their pretend family had reached the edge of its pretend life.

Wendy could love Neverland without choosing to stay there forever. Peter could love her company without knowing how to ask her not to leave. Above them, the guards had begun listening to a silence that did not feel right.
Hook's men were moving through the forest.

Chapter 8: The Light That Would Not Go Out. The pirates did not follow the familiar rules of the island's battles. Hook attacked before the guards expected him, and the sudden fight swept through the forest.
Down below, the children heard the noise but could not see what was happening. Then a signal sounded above them. Peter believed it meant that their friends had won.

He sent Wendy and the boys up through the trees, sure that the paths were safe. But the pirates had taken the signal for themselves. One by one, the children climbed out and were seized before they could warn those below.
Michael was carried away with the others. Wendy struggled to look back, hoping Peter would notice that nobody had called goodbye. The pirates dragged them toward the ship.
Peter, left alone, lay down to sleep. Hook found a way into the underground room and stood over his enemy. Sleeping Peter looked much smaller than the laughing boy the captain knew.
That only made Hook hate him more. Near the bed stood a cup of medicine Wendy had left for Peter. Hook added poison to it, then slipped away.
He expected the boy to do the rest without knowing there was a battle left to fight. Tinker Bell reached Peter after escaping the pirates' notice. She rang urgently beside his head until he woke.
At first he was annoyed that she would not let him sleep. Then he understood that Wendy and all the boys had been taken. He sprang up, ready to fly after them.
But before leaving, he remembered Wendy's medicine and reached for the cup. Tinker Bell darted between his hand and his mouth. She told him it was poisoned.
Peter would not believe that Hook had entered his home without his noticing. His pride made him trust his own certainty more than her warning. There was no time for another argument.
Tinker Bell drank the medicine herself before he could take it. "Why would you do that?" Peter cried. Her answering bells were so faint that he had to bend close to hear them.
All his clever tricks seemed useless beside a light that might go out. Her light began to weaken. Peter caught her, suddenly frightened by how little she weighed.

The fairy who had been fierce with jealousy had chosen to give everything for him. Now he could not command her light to burn brighter. He called out to children beyond the island, asking them to show that they believed in fairies.

Perhaps the plea could travel as far as the stories that brought children to Neverland in their sleep. In this strange adventure, the answer came as clapping. It grew louder, and Tinker Bell's light slowly strengthened.
Peter laughed with relief, but his voice had changed. He thanked her before rushing toward the door. The room still held the empty cup, a small ordinary object that had almost ended everything.
Peter had learned too late to believe the warning, but he had been given another chance to listen. He flew into the night, following the way to Hook's ship.
Chapter 9: Footsteps on the Pirate Ship. The ship lay dark on the water, with lanterns swinging above its deck. Wendy and the boys had been tied up while Hook prepared their punishment.

The captain offered the boys a chance to join his crew. Some looked at the pirates' weapons and wondered whether refusing would be the last brave thing they did. Hook noticed their hesitation and smiled.

"There is room for useful boys aboard my ship," he said. Wendy looked at the boys, hoping they could hear the threat hidden inside that invitation. But they would not leave one another to face the captain alone.
Wendy stood straight, although she was frightened. Hook disliked seeing children look at him without admiration. He spoke of making them walk the plank, a narrow board stretched over the sea.
Below it, the water waited without making a promise. The pirates gathered around, pleased to have an entertainment that did not put themselves in danger. Then a sound reached the ship.
Tick, tick, tick. Hook froze. His fine words disappeared, and he hurried away from the rail.
The pirates stared into the dark, expecting the crocodile's eyes to appear. But Peter had noticed that the animal's clock had stopped. He made the ticking sound himself as he approached the ship.
What frightened Hook protected Peter better than a shield. He climbed aboard while the captain hid, and slipped into the dark below the deck. One pirate was sent down and did not come back.
Another went after him. The ship's noisy confidence began to break apart. When a strange crowing sound rose from below, the pirates decided something unnatural had come among them.

Hook ordered men forward, but orders did not make their feet move faster. Peter used the confusion to reach the prisoners. Wendy recognized him before the others did, though he kept his voice low and his movements quick.

He cut the ropes around the boys and told them where to find weapons. For once they followed his instructions without demanding to know the whole plan. John steadied Michael, who was trying to look taller than he was.

The Lost Boys spread out, remembering that noisy courage was not always useful courage. Wendy stayed close, watching for anyone who might be left behind. Peter left her in a place where the pirates expected to find a prisoner.

He used a cloak to hide his own shape for the next part of the trick. Hook returned to the deck, determined to prove that he was still captain of this ship. But the children were free, the darkness had become an ally, and his men no longer knew whom they should fear most.

A fight broke out before Hook could understand how completely the night had changed. The boys fought for their lives and for the way home. Peter fought with the sharp delight of someone who had finally found his favorite game.
Wendy saw both kinds of courage and understood that they did not feel the same inside. Across the deck, Hook saw the boy he hated. This time there was no forest, rock, or secret voice between them.
They faced each other beneath the swinging lamps.

Chapter 10: A Captain's Last Battle. Hook's sword flashed, and Peter moved aside so lightly that he seemed hardly attached to the deck. Around them, the fight continued, but the captain's eyes stayed fixed on the boy.

He wanted to end the laughter that had followed him through so many defeats. Peter met his attacks quickly, using his small size and sudden movements. Hook had strength, experience, and a terrible reach.

Peter had speed and the unsettling confidence of someone who could forget fear before it grew roots. The captain tried to find a weakness in that confidence. He demanded to know what kind of creature Peter really was.

Peter answered with the bright, careless certainty of youth. He belonged to everything beginning again, to games and new days, and to the hope that tomorrow would be even better. Hook had built his pride out of being a gentleman and a captain.
Before this boy, those titles seemed suddenly heavy. Still, he fought hard. His hook caught and tore, his sword struck, and Peter had to keep moving.
The boy did not win simply because the story liked him better. He watched, waited, and took the openings the captain gave him. At last the fight pushed Hook toward the edge of the ship.
Beyond the rail, the sea looked black. The crocodile was waiting there, with no clock left to announce it. Hook saw that the end of his great fear had arrived without its familiar sound.

Even then, he wanted one last victory of manners. He tried to make Peter behave badly, so that the captain could leave the world believing himself the better gentleman. Peter kicked instead of offering the kind of finish Hook expected.
Hook fell into the sea, carrying his strange satisfaction with him. The crocodile closed over the captain, and the water settled again. For a little while, nobody spoke.

The danger that had shaped their days had ended, but the ending was darker than the beginning of a game. Then the boys began to cheer. The surviving pirates were beaten, and Smee managed to escape rather than share his captain's fate.

Peter took command of the ship with immediate pleasure. He tried on the idea of being captain as easily as another boy might try on a hat. Before long he was giving orders with some of Hook's grand manner.

Wendy noticed, and wondered how quickly a person could begin resembling an enemy after taking his place. "Captain," she said, choosing the title because she knew it would please him. Peter turned with a grand movement of his new coat.
"We still need to go home," she reminded him. He sighed as if homes were forever getting in the way of important business. She reminded Peter that they had a destination.

London was not a word to be put aside until another adventure had finished. The boys set the ship toward home under his direction. They climbed ropes, watched the sea, and slept wherever exhaustion found them.
Wendy checked on Michael and John, grateful each time she found them safe. She had once imagined that going away was the brave part. Now she knew that choosing to return could ask for courage too.
Ahead of them lay an ordinary house, an open window, and people who had been waiting longer than the children understood.
Chapter 11: The Window Still Open. In London, Mrs. Darling had kept the children's window open. Cold nights came, and she covered the empty beds, but she would not close the way back.

Mr. Darling blamed himself for putting Nana outside on the night the children disappeared. In his misery, he began sleeping in the dog's kennel. It was an uncomfortable punishment, and quite impossible to explain properly to visitors.

Nana kept her watch, though there were no small feet to follow upstairs. The house had all its usual rooms and almost none of its usual sounds. Before Wendy and the others arrived, Peter flew ahead with Tinker Bell.
He found the open window and thought of the friends he was about to lose. If the children could not get in, perhaps they would have to return to Neverland with him. He shut the window.
For a moment, the plan seemed wonderfully simple. Then he saw Mrs. Darling. She sat close to the children's room, worn by waiting and still listening for sounds that did not come.
Peter looked at her and tried to make himself feel annoyed instead of troubled. Why should a mother have Wendy when he wanted her too? But the sight of her sadness would not leave him alone.
It followed him even when he turned his face away. At last he opened the window again. Giving someone a way home was harder than teaching her to fly.

He slipped away before the others could see what he had nearly done. Wendy, John, and Michael came through the window into their old room. Their beds looked familiar, but some details already felt strangely distant.
Michael wondered whether he had been there before. Wendy felt a sharp ache at hearing the question. She had brought him home just in time for home to become real again.

They climbed into their beds, hoping to surprise their mother. When Mrs. Darling entered, she looked at them and did not cry out. She had dreamed of seeing them there so often that she thought this was another dream refusing to end.
Wendy called to her. Then John called, and Michael reached out his arms. Their mother's doubt broke, and she gathered them close.

The room filled with voices, tears, laughter, and Nana's delighted movements. Mr. Darling emerged from the kennel, and the children found him easier to recognize when he was standing upright. The Lost Boys waited nearby, afraid there might be no welcome left for them.

Wendy explained who they were. Her parents opened their home to the boys, although finding enough beds would require more than a little thought. Peter watched from outside, keeping himself beyond the warmth he had made possible.
Mrs. Darling invited him in too. She offered care, a home, and the ordinary future of growing older. Peter asked about school, work, and becoming a man.

"Would I have to sit at a desk?" he asked. Mrs. Darling smiled and said that there would be many things to learn. Peter had heard enough to suspect that even this kind woman could not offer a home without a future attached to it.
The answers made him step back. He would not stay, but he asked whether Wendy could visit him sometimes. An agreement was made for a short return to Neverland in the spring.
Wendy stood at the window while Peter disappeared into the sky. She was happy to be home, and still sad that he could not be happy there beside her.

Chapter 12: The Girl Who Grew Up. The Lost Boys learned the unfamiliar habits of ordinary life. There were lessons to attend, clothes to keep tidy, and rules that did not change merely because Peter found them boring.
For a time, they could still fly. Then daily life made that old skill seem less necessary, and gradually it left them. John and Michael grew older beside them.

Wendy changed too, although the changes were so small each day that she did not always notice them. Peter returned the first spring, and she went with him for a short visit. She cleaned, mended, and listened to adventures as if no time had passed.

But time had passed for Wendy, even if Peter could not feel it. He did not remember Captain Hook as clearly as she expected. When she asked about Tinker Bell, his answer showed how quickly old companions slipped out of his mind.

Fairies did not live long, he said, and another adventure could take the place of yesterday's friend. Wendy felt the hurt of remembering someone who had already been forgotten by another. Peter could keep the freshness of a beginning, but he could not keep everything that made a friendship whole.
Some springs he returned, and some he forgot. Wendy waited, then learned to carry on with her own days. School gave way to other responsibilities.

The boys became grown men, and Neverland moved into the place where childhood memories are kept. Wendy married and had a daughter called Jane. Jane loved hearing about the flying boy and the island beyond the night.

She listened from her bed, asking questions at exactly the places where Wendy used to ask them. One evening, Peter appeared at the window again. He came ready to take Wendy away, as if the years outside the room had been no longer than a game.
The woman waiting there was not the child he expected. Wendy tried to explain gently. She had grown up.
"You said you would come back," Peter said. "I did come back," Wendy answered. "But I could not keep being the same age while I waited."

Peter stared, searching her face for the girl he had left behind. He had refused change so completely that he could not understand how she had let it happen. For once, his proud little manner fell apart.
He cried. Wendy could not make herself small again to spare him the pain. She could only stay beside him while he discovered that wanting time to stop did not stop it for everyone else.
Then Jane woke and saw the boy she knew from her mother's stories. To her, he was not an ending. He was the beginning of an adventure.

Peter lifted his head, and the lightness returned to his face. With Wendy's permission, Jane went with him to Neverland for a visit. Wendy watched them leave through the window she no longer needed for her own escape.

Her sadness and her happiness stood side by side. Later, Jane grew up too, and her daughter Margaret heard the same wonderful stories. Peter returned for another child, while the children he had known became part of a history he could not hold.
Neverland kept its forests, pirates, and impossible skies. The Darling family kept something different: people who remembered, loved, and changed together. Peter could remain a boy forever.

Wendy had chosen a life that could become larger than childhood. Neither the open window nor the distant island erased the cost of those choices. But the stories continued, passing from one growing child to the next.

stories.title: Treasure Island
stories.synopsis: 一张藏宝图把吉姆带上海盗的船。在冒险中，他必须学会判断信任、勇气和承诺。
stories.credits: 原著：Robert Louis Stevenson；原版插画：Louis Rhead。采用 Project Gutenberg 原版。本站简明英文改写与中文翻译为新编，CC BY 4.0；不代表原著全文，也没有正式蓝思测评。
stories.translationNote: 12 章完整主要故事线的节选改写；采用常用词和短句，保留成长与选择。

chapters.title: A Friendly Man with One Leg

picturePages.text: Treasure Island.

sentences.en: Treasure Island.
sentences.zh: 金银岛：简明英文改写版。

picturePages.text: Chapter 1: The Sailor at the Inn. My name is Jim Hawkins, and this is the story of how I found treasure. My parents kept a small inn near the sea.

sentences.en: Chapter 1: The Sailor at the Inn.
sentences.zh: 第1章：旅店里的水手。

sentences.en: My name is Jim Hawkins, and this is the story of how I found treasure.
sentences.zh: 我叫吉姆·霍金斯，这是我找到宝藏的故事。

sentences.en: My parents kept a small inn near the sea.
sentences.zh: 我的父母在海边经营一家小旅店。

picturePages.text: One day, an old sailor arrived with a heavy sea chest. He called himself the captain, but his real name was Billy Bones. He drank too much and sang loud songs about pirates.

sentences.en: One day, an old sailor arrived with a heavy sea chest.
sentences.zh: 一天，一个老水手带着沉重的航海箱来了。

sentences.en: He called himself the captain, but his real name was Billy Bones.
sentences.zh: 他自称船长，但真名是比利·博恩斯。

sentences.en: He drank too much and sang loud songs about pirates.
sentences.zh: 他喝酒过量，还大声唱着海盗的歌。

picturePages.text: He paid me to watch for a sailor with one leg. I began to see that man in my dreams. Billy frightened our guests, but Doctor Livesey was not afraid of him.

sentences.en: He paid me to watch for a sailor with one leg.
sentences.zh: 他付钱让我留意一个只有一条腿的水手。

sentences.en: I began to see that man in my dreams.
sentences.zh: 我开始在梦里见到那个人。

sentences.en: Billy frightened our guests, but Doctor Livesey was not afraid of him.
sentences.zh: 比利吓坏了客人，但利弗西医生不怕他。

picturePages.text: The doctor warned him that too much drink would kill him. Then a stranger called Black Dog came to the inn. He and Billy fought, and Black Dog ran away.

sentences.en: The doctor warned him that too much drink would kill him.
sentences.zh: 医生警告他，喝酒过量会害死他。

sentences.en: Then a stranger called Black Dog came to the inn.
sentences.zh: 后来，一个叫黑狗的陌生人来到旅店。

sentences.en: He and Billy fought, and Black Dog ran away.
sentences.zh: 他和比利打了一架，黑狗逃走了。

picturePages.text: Billy fell ill, and I understood that his past had found him.

sentences.en: Billy fell ill, and I understood that his past had found him.
sentences.zh: 比利病倒了，我明白，他想逃避的过去找上门了。

picturePages.text: Chapter 2: The Map in the Chest. My father died while Billy was staying with us. My mother and I were grieving, and we needed money to keep the inn.

sentences.en: Chapter 2: The Map in the Chest.
sentences.zh: 第2章：箱子里的地图。

sentences.en: My father died while Billy was staying with us.
sentences.zh: 比利住在我们这里的时候，我父亲去世了。

sentences.en: My mother and I were grieving, and we needed money to keep the inn.
sentences.zh: 母亲和我十分悲伤，还需要钱来维持旅店。

picturePages.text: One evening, a blind man made me lead him to Billy. He put a small piece of paper into Billy's hand. It was the black spot, a warning from the pirates.

sentences.en: One evening, a blind man made me lead him to Billy.
sentences.zh: 一天傍晚，一个盲人逼我带他去见比利。

sentences.en: He put a small piece of paper into Billy's hand.
sentences.zh: 他把一小张纸放进比利手中。

sentences.en: It was the black spot, a warning from the pirates.
sentences.zh: 那是黑点，是海盗发出的警告。

picturePages.text: Billy tried to stand up, but he fell and died. Mother opened his chest to take the money he owed us. She refused to take more, even though we were in danger.

sentences.en: Billy tried to stand up, but he fell and died.
sentences.zh: 比利想站起来，却倒下死了。

sentences.en: Mother opened his chest to take the money he owed us.
sentences.zh: 母亲打开他的箱子，取他欠我们的钱。

sentences.en: She refused to take more, even though we were in danger.
sentences.zh: 尽管我们身处危险，她也不肯多拿。

picturePages.text: I took a packet of papers, and we escaped before the pirates arrived. Later, I showed the papers to the doctor and Squire Trelawney. Inside was a map showing where Captain Flint had buried his gold.

sentences.en: I took a packet of papers, and we escaped before the pirates arrived.
sentences.zh: 我拿走一包文件，我们在海盗到来之前逃走了。

sentences.en: Later, I showed the papers to the doctor and Squire Trelawney.
sentences.zh: 后来，我把文件交给医生和乡绅特里劳尼看。

sentences.en: Inside was a map showing where Captain Flint had buried his gold.
sentences.zh: 里面是一张地图，标出了弗林特船长埋藏黄金的地方。

picturePages.text: The squire promised to buy a ship, and suddenly my life became an adventure.

sentences.en: The squire promised to buy a ship, and suddenly my life became an adventure.
sentences.zh: 乡绅答应买一艘船，我的生活突然变成了一场冒险。

picturePages.text: Chapter 3: A Friendly Man with One Leg. Our ship was called the Hispaniola. In Bristol, the squire hired a cook named Long John Silver.

sentences.en: Chapter 3: A Friendly Man with One Leg.
sentences.zh: 第3章：友好的独腿人。

sentences.en: Our ship was called the Hispaniola.
sentences.zh: 我们的船叫伊斯帕尼奥拉号。

sentences.en: In Bristol, the squire hired a cook named Long John Silver.
sentences.zh: 在布里斯托尔，乡绅雇了一个名叫长约翰·西尔弗的厨师。

picturePages.text: Silver had one leg, a warm smile, and a parrot on his shoulder. His parrot shouted, "Pieces of eight!" I remembered Billy's warning, but Silver seemed too kind to be dangerous.

sentences.en: Silver had one leg, a warm smile, and a parrot on his shoulder.
sentences.zh: 西尔弗只有一条腿，笑容亲切，肩上停着一只鹦鹉。

sentences.en: His parrot shouted, "Pieces of eight!"
sentences.zh: 他的鹦鹉大喊：“八里亚尔银币！”

sentences.en: I remembered Billy's warning, but Silver seemed too kind to be dangerous.
sentences.zh: 我想起比利的警告，但西尔弗看起来太友善，不像危险人物。

picturePages.text: He told me about ships and treated me like a friend. He also helped the squire find sailors for our voyage. Captain Smollett did not like the way the voyage had been planned.

sentences.en: He told me about ships and treated me like a friend.
sentences.zh: 他给我讲船上的事情，像朋友一样对待我。

sentences.en: He also helped the squire find sailors for our voyage.
sentences.zh: 他还帮乡绅寻找航行需要的水手。

sentences.en: Captain Smollett did not like the way the voyage had been planned.
sentences.zh: 斯莫利特船长不喜欢这次航行的安排方式。

picturePages.text: The squire had talked freely about the treasure, and everyone knew our secret. The captain moved the guns and powder to a safer place on the ship. I thought he was too strict, while Silver seemed wonderful.

sentences.en: The squire had talked freely about the treasure, and everyone knew our secret.
sentences.zh: 乡绅随意谈论宝藏，所有人都知道了我们的秘密。

sentences.en: The captain moved the guns and powder to a safer place on the ship.
sentences.zh: 船长把枪和火药移到了船上更安全的地方。

sentences.en: I thought he was too strict, while Silver seemed wonderful.
sentences.zh: 我觉得船长太严厉了，而西尔弗很好。

picturePages.text: I had not yet learned how easily a friendly face can hide a dangerous plan.

sentences.en: I had not yet learned how easily a friendly face can hide a dangerous plan.
sentences.zh: 我还不知道，友好的面孔多么容易掩盖危险的计划。

picturePages.text: Chapter 4: Inside the Apple Barrel. One night, I climbed into a barrel to find an apple. Before I could climb out, Silver sat down beside it.

sentences.en: Chapter 4: Inside the Apple Barrel.
sentences.zh: 第4章：苹果桶里。

sentences.en: One night, I climbed into a barrel to find an apple.
sentences.zh: 一天夜里，我爬进桶里找苹果。

sentences.en: Before I could climb out, Silver sat down beside it.
sentences.zh: 我还没爬出来，西尔弗就在旁边坐下了。

picturePages.text: He began talking to two sailors, and I stayed very still. Silver had sailed with Captain Flint, and many of our sailors were pirates. They planned to let the captain find the treasure first.

sentences.en: He began talking to two sailors, and I stayed very still.
sentences.zh: 他开始和两个水手交谈，我一动也不敢动。

sentences.en: Silver had sailed with Captain Flint, and many of our sailors were pirates.
sentences.zh: 西尔弗曾和弗林特船长一起航行，我们的许多水手都是海盗。

sentences.en: They planned to let the captain find the treasure first.
sentences.zh: 他们打算先让船长找到宝藏。

picturePages.text: Then they would take the ship and kill anyone who stood in their way. The man I trusted was quietly planning to destroy us. My heart beat hard, but I waited until the men had left.

sentences.en: Then they would take the ship and kill anyone who stood in their way.
sentences.zh: 然后他们就要夺船，杀死挡路的人。

sentences.en: The man I trusted was quietly planning to destroy us.
sentences.zh: 我信任的人正在悄悄谋划害死我们。

sentences.en: My heart beat hard, but I waited until the men had left.
sentences.zh: 我的心怦怦直跳，但我一直等到那些人离开。

picturePages.text: I told the doctor, the squire, and the captain what I had heard. There were far more pirates than loyal men on board. We agreed to smile, keep our secret, and wait for a chance to act.

sentences.en: I told the doctor, the squire, and the captain what I had heard.
sentences.zh: 我把听到的事情告诉医生、乡绅和船长。

sentences.en: There were far more pirates than loyal men on board.
sentences.zh: 船上海盗的人数远远超过可靠的人。

sentences.en: We agreed to smile, keep our secret, and wait for a chance to act.
sentences.zh: 我们决定面带微笑，保守秘密，等待行动的机会。

picturePages.text: Now every friendly word from Silver made me feel cold.

sentences.en: Now every friendly word from Silver made me feel cold.
sentences.zh: 现在，西尔弗每说一句友好的话，都让我感到心寒。

picturePages.text: Chapter 5: The Man in the Trees. When we reached the island, the captain let some sailors go ashore. I slipped into their boat because I wanted to see the island for myself.

sentences.en: Chapter 5: The Man in the Trees.
sentences.zh: 第5章：树林里的人。

sentences.en: When we reached the island, the captain let some sailors go ashore.
sentences.zh: 我们到达岛上后，船长让一些水手上岸。

sentences.en: I slipped into their boat because I wanted to see the island for myself.
sentences.zh: 我溜进他们的船里，想亲眼看看岛屿。

picturePages.text: Once we landed, I ran into the trees. I heard Silver arguing with Tom, an honest sailor. Tom refused to join the pirates, and Silver killed him.

sentences.en: Once we landed, I ran into the trees.
sentences.zh: 一上岸，我就跑进树林。

sentences.en: I heard Silver arguing with Tom, an honest sailor.
sentences.zh: 我听见西尔弗和一个正直的水手汤姆争吵。

sentences.en: Tom refused to join the pirates, and Silver killed him.
sentences.zh: 汤姆拒绝加入海盗，西尔弗杀了他。

picturePages.text: I ran away in fear, no longer doubting what Silver could do. Then a thin man appeared among the trees and spoke my name. He was Ben Gunn, a sailor left on the island three years before.

sentences.en: I ran away in fear, no longer doubting what Silver could do.
sentences.zh: 我害怕地逃走了，再也不怀疑西尔弗会做出什么事。

sentences.en: Then a thin man appeared among the trees and spoke my name.
sentences.zh: 接着，一个瘦瘦的人出现在树林里，问起我的名字。

sentences.en: He was Ben Gunn, a sailor left on the island three years before.
sentences.zh: 他叫本·冈恩，是三年前被留在岛上的水手。

picturePages.text: He had survived alone, but he longed to go home and eat cheese again. Ben knew Silver, and he knew a great deal about Flint's treasure. He offered to help if the doctor would take him home.

sentences.en: He had survived alone, but he longed to go home and eat cheese again.
sentences.zh: 他独自活了下来，但渴望回家，再吃到奶酪。

sentences.en: Ben knew Silver, and he knew a great deal about Flint's treasure.
sentences.zh: 本认识西尔弗，也知道许多关于弗林特宝藏的事。

sentences.en: He offered to help if the doctor would take him home.
sentences.zh: 他提出，只要医生带他回家，他就愿意帮忙。

picturePages.text: Before we parted, he told me where he had hidden a little boat.

sentences.en: Before we parted, he told me where he had hidden a little boat.
sentences.zh: 分开之前，他告诉我他把一条小船藏在了哪里。

picturePages.text: Chapter 6: The Wooden Fort. While I was exploring, the doctor and our loyal men left the ship. They carried food and guns to an old wooden fort with fresh water.

sentences.en: Chapter 6: The Wooden Fort.
sentences.zh: 第6章：木头堡垒。

sentences.en: While I was exploring, the doctor and our loyal men left the ship.
sentences.zh: 我探索岛屿的时候，医生和可靠的伙伴们离开了大船。

sentences.en: They carried food and guns to an old wooden fort with fresh water.
sentences.zh: 他们带着食物和枪，来到一座有淡水的旧木头堡垒。

picturePages.text: I found them there and told the doctor about Ben Gunn. The next morning, Silver arrived carrying a white flag. He offered to let us live if we gave him the treasure map.

sentences.en: I found them there and told the doctor about Ben Gunn.
sentences.zh: 我在那里找到他们，并把本·冈恩的事情告诉医生。

sentences.en: The next morning, Silver arrived carrying a white flag.
sentences.zh: 第二天早上，西尔弗举着白旗来了。

sentences.en: He offered to let us live if we gave him the treasure map.
sentences.zh: 他提出，只要我们交出藏宝图，就让我们活命。

picturePages.text: Captain Smollett refused to trust a promise from a man who had betrayed us. Silver left in anger, and soon the pirates attacked. We fought from behind the wooden walls.

sentences.en: Captain Smollett refused to trust a promise from a man who had betrayed us.
sentences.zh: 斯莫利特船长不肯相信背叛我们的人的承诺。

sentences.en: Silver left in anger, and soon the pirates attacked.
sentences.zh: 西尔弗愤怒地离开，很快海盗就发起了进攻。

sentences.en: We fought from behind the wooden walls.
sentences.zh: 我们躲在木墙后面战斗。

picturePages.text: We held the fort, but several men died and the captain was badly hurt. The island no longer felt like a place for a wonderful adventure. People were paying for the treasure with their lives.

sentences.en: We held the fort, but several men died and the captain was badly hurt.
sentences.zh: 我们守住了堡垒，但有几个人死了，船长也受了重伤。

sentences.en: The island no longer felt like a place for a wonderful adventure.
sentences.zh: 这座岛再也不像一个充满美妙冒险的地方。

sentences.en: People were paying for the treasure with their lives.
sentences.zh: 人们正在用生命为宝藏付出代价。

picturePages.text: I wanted to help, but I was about to make another dangerous choice alone.

sentences.en: I wanted to help, but I was about to make another dangerous choice alone.
sentences.zh: 我想帮忙，却又要独自作出一个危险的决定。

picturePages.text: Chapter 7: A Small Boat at Night. The fort was hot, and I grew tired of waiting. Without asking anyone, I took some food and slipped away.

sentences.en: Chapter 7: A Small Boat at Night.
sentences.zh: 第7章：夜里的小船。

sentences.en: The fort was hot, and I grew tired of waiting.
sentences.zh: 堡垒里很热，我也厌倦了等待。

sentences.en: Without asking anyone, I took some food and slipped away.
sentences.zh: 我没有问任何人，带着一点食物就溜走了。

picturePages.text: I found Ben Gunn's little boat beneath a white rock. It was light and round, and it was difficult to control. After dark, I pushed it into the sea and moved towards the Hispaniola.

sentences.en: I found Ben Gunn's little boat beneath a white rock.
sentences.zh: 我在一块白色岩石下面找到了本·冈恩的小船。

sentences.en: It was light and round, and it was difficult to control.
sentences.zh: 它又轻又圆，很难控制。

sentences.en: After dark, I pushed it into the sea and moved towards the Hispaniola.
sentences.zh: 天黑后，我把它推入海中，朝伊斯帕尼奥拉号划去。

picturePages.text: Only two pirates were on the ship, and they were drinking and fighting. I cut the rope that held the ship in place. The ship began to drift, and I hoped the pirates would lose it.

sentences.en: Only two pirates were on the ship, and they were drinking and fighting.
sentences.zh: 船上只有两个海盗，他们正在喝酒、打架。

sentences.en: I cut the rope that held the ship in place.
sentences.zh: 我割断了固定大船的绳索。

sentences.en: The ship began to drift, and I hoped the pirates would lose it.
sentences.zh: 大船开始漂走，我希望海盗就此失去它。

picturePages.text: But the sea also carried my small boat away from shore. Waves rose around me, and I could not make the boat obey. I was alone in the dark because I had refused to ask for help.

sentences.en: But the sea also carried my small boat away from shore.
sentences.zh: 可海水也把我的小船带离了岸边。

sentences.en: Waves rose around me, and I could not make the boat obey.
sentences.zh: 浪头在我四周升起，我无法控制小船。

sentences.en: I was alone in the dark because I had refused to ask for help.
sentences.zh: 我独自在黑暗中，因为我没有向别人寻求帮助。

picturePages.text: At last I fell asleep, too tired to fight the sea any longer.

sentences.en: At last I fell asleep, too tired to fight the sea any longer.
sentences.zh: 最后，我睡着了，累得再也无法和海浪抗争。

picturePages.text: Chapter 8: The Ship Is Mine. In the morning, I saw the Hispaniola drifting nearby. I managed to climb on board before my little boat sank.

sentences.en: Chapter 8: The Ship Is Mine.
sentences.zh: 第8章：船属于我了。

sentences.en: In the morning, I saw the Hispaniola drifting nearby.
sentences.zh: 早上，我看见伊斯帕尼奥拉号在附近漂着。

sentences.en: I managed to climb on board before my little boat sank.
sentences.zh: 我在小船沉没之前，设法爬上了大船。

picturePages.text: One pirate was dead, and the other, Israel Hands, was badly hurt. I took down the pirate flag and said that the ship was mine. Hands offered to help me sail into the sheltered North Inlet.

sentences.en: One pirate was dead, and the other, Israel Hands, was badly hurt.
sentences.zh: 一个海盗已经死了，另一个叫伊斯雷尔·汉兹，受了重伤。

sentences.en: I took down the pirate flag and said that the ship was mine.
sentences.zh: 我取下海盗旗，宣布这艘船属于我了。

sentences.en: Hands offered to help me sail into the sheltered North Inlet.
sentences.zh: 汉兹提出帮我把船驶入避风的北边海湾。

picturePages.text: I needed his knowledge, but I watched him carefully. While I was busy with the ship, he hid a knife. When we reached shallow water, he suddenly came after me.

sentences.en: I needed his knowledge, but I watched him carefully.
sentences.zh: 我需要他的经验，但也小心地盯着他。

sentences.en: While I was busy with the ship, he hid a knife.
sentences.zh: 我忙着操控船时，他藏起了一把刀。

sentences.en: When we reached shallow water, he suddenly came after me.
sentences.zh: 我们到达浅水处时，他突然向我扑来。

picturePages.text: I climbed up the mast, and he threw his knife into my shoulder. I fired my pistol, and Hands fell into the sea. Shaking with fear, I freed myself and covered the wound.

sentences.en: I climbed up the mast, and he threw his knife into my shoulder.
sentences.zh: 我爬上桅杆，他掷出的刀刺中了我的肩膀。

sentences.en: I fired my pistol, and Hands fell into the sea.
sentences.zh: 我开了枪，汉兹掉进了海里。

sentences.en: Shaking with fear, I freed myself and covered the wound.
sentences.zh: 我害怕得浑身发抖，挣脱出来，把伤口包扎好。

picturePages.text: I had saved the ship, but I did not feel like a happy hero.

sentences.en: I had saved the ship, but I did not feel like a happy hero.
sentences.zh: 我救下了大船，却没有觉得自己是个快乐的英雄。

picturePages.text: Chapter 9: Among the Pirates. That night, I walked back to the fort, hoping to find my friends. The place was dark, and I stepped inside quietly.

sentences.en: Chapter 9: Among the Pirates.
sentences.zh: 第9章：身处海盗之中。

sentences.en: That night, I walked back to the fort, hoping to find my friends.
sentences.zh: 那天夜里，我走回堡垒，希望找到朋友们。

sentences.en: The place was dark, and I stepped inside quietly.
sentences.zh: 那里黑漆漆的，我轻轻走了进去。

picturePages.text: Suddenly, Silver's parrot cried out above my head. The pirates had taken the fort, and I was their prisoner. Silver told me that the doctor had given them the fort and the map.

sentences.en: Suddenly, Silver's parrot cried out above my head.
sentences.zh: 突然，西尔弗的鹦鹉在我头顶叫了起来。

sentences.en: The pirates had taken the fort, and I was their prisoner.
sentences.zh: 海盗已经占领了堡垒，我成了他们的俘虏。

sentences.en: Silver told me that the doctor had given them the fort and the map.
sentences.zh: 西尔弗告诉我，医生把堡垒和地图交给了他们。

picturePages.text: I could not understand why my friends had done this. The pirates wanted to kill me, but Silver stood between us. He hoped I would speak for him if he ever faced a trial.

sentences.en: I could not understand why my friends had done this.
sentences.zh: 我无法理解朋友们为什么这样做。

sentences.en: The pirates wanted to kill me, but Silver stood between us.
sentences.zh: 海盗想杀我，但西尔弗挡在了我们之间。

sentences.en: He hoped I would speak for him if he ever faced a trial.
sentences.zh: 他希望，如果将来他受到审判，我能为他说话。

picturePages.text: I told him that I had heard his plan and hidden the ship. His men grew angry and gave him another black spot. But Silver showed them the map and won back their trust.

sentences.en: I told him that I had heard his plan and hidden the ship.
sentences.zh: 我告诉他，我听见了他的计划，也藏起了大船。

sentences.en: His men grew angry and gave him another black spot.
sentences.zh: 他的手下愤怒起来，又给了他一个黑点。

sentences.en: But Silver showed them the map and won back their trust.
sentences.zh: 但西尔弗拿出地图，又赢回了他们的信任。

picturePages.text: He had protected me, yet I knew he was also protecting himself.

sentences.en: He had protected me, yet I knew he was also protecting himself.
sentences.zh: 他保护了我，但我知道，他也是在保护自己。

picturePages.text: Chapter 10: A Promise to Keep. The next morning, Doctor Livesey came to treat the sick pirates. He helped them even though they were his enemies.

sentences.en: Chapter 10: A Promise to Keep.
sentences.zh: 第10章：必须守住的承诺。

sentences.en: The next morning, Doctor Livesey came to treat the sick pirates.
sentences.zh: 第二天早上，利弗西医生来给生病的海盗看病。

sentences.en: He helped them even though they were his enemies.
sentences.zh: 即使他们是敌人，他也帮助他们。

picturePages.text: When he saw me, he looked both relieved and angry. I had left my friends without warning and put myself in danger. I told him that I was sorry and that the ship was safe in the North Inlet.

sentences.en: When he saw me, he looked both relieved and angry.
sentences.zh: 看见我时，他既松了一口气，又很生气。

sentences.en: I had left my friends without warning and put myself in danger.
sentences.zh: 我没有打招呼就离开朋友们，把自己置于危险之中。

sentences.en: I told him that I was sorry and that the ship was safe in the North Inlet.
sentences.zh: 我向他道歉，并告诉他大船安全地停在北边海湾。

picturePages.text: The doctor wanted me to run away with him. But I had promised Silver that I would not escape. I did not want to become a person whose words meant nothing.

sentences.en: The doctor wanted me to run away with him.
sentences.zh: 医生想让我和他一起逃走。

sentences.en: But I had promised Silver that I would not escape.
sentences.zh: 可我已经向西尔弗保证不会逃跑。

sentences.en: I did not want to become a person whose words meant nothing.
sentences.zh: 我不想成为一个说话不算数的人。

picturePages.text: The doctor listened, although it was hard for him to leave me there. He asked Silver to keep me safe and warned him to be careful at the treasure. The doctor seemed to know something that neither of us understood.

sentences.en: The doctor listened, although it was hard for him to leave me there.
sentences.zh: 医生听完了，尽管把我留在那里让他很难受。

sentences.en: He asked Silver to keep me safe and warned him to be careful at the treasure.
sentences.zh: 他要求西尔弗保护我，并警告他寻宝时要小心。

sentences.en: The doctor seemed to know something that neither of us understood.
sentences.zh: 医生似乎知道一些我们俩都不明白的事情。

picturePages.text: As he walked away, I hoped that keeping my promise was not a terrible mistake.

sentences.en: As he walked away, I hoped that keeping my promise was not a terrible mistake.
sentences.zh: 他走远时，我希望守住承诺不会是一个可怕的错误。

picturePages.text: Chapter 11: The Empty Treasure Pit. Silver led the pirates into the forest, and I walked beside him. We found a skeleton with an arm pointing towards the treasure.

sentences.en: Chapter 11: The Empty Treasure Pit.
sentences.zh: 第11章：空空的藏宝坑。

sentences.en: Silver led the pirates into the forest, and I walked beside him.
sentences.zh: 西尔弗带着海盗们走进树林，我走在他旁边。

sentences.en: We found a skeleton with an arm pointing towards the treasure.
sentences.zh: 我们发现一具骷髅，它的一只手臂指向宝藏的方向。

picturePages.text: Flint had left it there as a sign, and the men were afraid. Then a strange voice rose from the trees, singing Flint's old song. Some pirates thought that a dead man had come back.

sentences.en: Flint had left it there as a sign, and the men were afraid.
sentences.zh: 弗林特把它留在那里当路标，海盗们十分害怕。

sentences.en: Then a strange voice rose from the trees, singing Flint's old song.
sentences.zh: 接着，树林里传来奇怪的声音，唱着弗林特过去的歌。

sentences.en: Some pirates thought that a dead man had come back.
sentences.zh: 一些海盗以为死人回来了。

picturePages.text: Silver kept them moving, but even he looked worried. At last we reached the place marked on the map. The treasure pit was empty, with only a few broken boards inside.

sentences.en: Silver kept them moving, but even he looked worried.
sentences.zh: 西尔弗让他们继续前进，但连他也显得不安。

sentences.en: At last we reached the place marked on the map.
sentences.zh: 最后，我们到达了地图上标出的地点。

sentences.en: The treasure pit was empty, with only a few broken boards inside.
sentences.zh: 藏宝坑空空的，里面只有几块破木板。

picturePages.text: The pirates turned on Silver, believing that he had tricked them. Before they could attack us, shots came from the trees. The doctor, Ben Gunn, and our friend Gray rushed out and saved us.

sentences.en: The pirates turned on Silver, believing that he had tricked them.
sentences.zh: 海盗们转而攻击西尔弗，以为他欺骗了他们。

sentences.en: Before they could attack us, shots came from the trees.
sentences.zh: 在他们动手之前，树林里响起了枪声。

sentences.en: The doctor, Ben Gunn, and our friend Gray rushed out and saved us.
sentences.zh: 医生、本·冈恩和我们的朋友格雷冲出来救了我们。

picturePages.text: Ben had found and moved the gold long before we arrived, and the strange voice was his.

sentences.en: Ben had found and moved the gold long before we arrived, and the strange voice was his.
sentences.zh: 本早在我们到来之前就找到了黄金并搬走了它，那奇怪的声音也是他发出的。

picturePages.text: Chapter 12: What We Took Home. Ben led us to his cave, where the gold lay in great piles. The doctor had learned his secret and given the pirates a useless map.

sentences.en: Chapter 12: What We Took Home.
sentences.zh: 第12章：我们带回家的东西。

sentences.en: Ben led us to his cave, where the gold lay in great piles.
sentences.zh: 本带我们来到他的洞穴，黄金在那里堆成了大堆。

sentences.en: The doctor had learned his secret and given the pirates a useless map.
sentences.zh: 医生知道了他的秘密，所以给了海盗一张已经无用的地图。

picturePages.text: For days, we carried the heavy treasure to our ship. Silver worked hard beside us, always watching for his next chance. We left three surviving pirates on the island with food, tools, and medicine.

sentences.en: For days, we carried the heavy treasure to our ship.
sentences.zh: 好几天里，我们把沉重的宝藏搬到船上。

sentences.en: Silver worked hard beside us, always watching for his next chance.
sentences.zh: 西尔弗在我们身边卖力干活，始终寻找下一个机会。

sentences.en: We left three surviving pirates on the island with food, tools, and medicine.
sentences.zh: 我们给三个活下来的海盗留下食物、工具和药物，把他们留在岛上。

picturePages.text: Then we sailed away from the place where so many people had died. At a port on our way home, Silver escaped with a bag of money. He had saved my life, but that did not erase the cruel things he had done.

sentences.en: Then we sailed away from the place where so many people had died.
sentences.zh: 然后我们驶离了这个许多人丧生的地方。

sentences.en: At a port on our way home, Silver escaped with a bag of money.
sentences.zh: 回家途中，在一座港口，西尔弗带着一袋钱逃走了。

sentences.en: He had saved my life, but that did not erase the cruel things he had done.
sentences.zh: 他救过我的命，但这不能抹去他做过的残酷事情。

picturePages.text: We each received a share of the treasure, and I returned to my mother. The money made our lives easier, but it could not bring back the people we had lost. Sometimes I still hear the sea in my dreams and the parrot crying for silver coins.

sentences.en: We each received a share of the treasure, and I returned to my mother.
sentences.zh: 我们每个人都分到了一份宝藏，我回到母亲身边。

sentences.en: The money made our lives easier, but it could not bring back the people we had lost.
sentences.zh: 钱让我们的生活轻松了一些，但无法让失去的人回来。

sentences.en: Sometimes I still hear the sea in my dreams and the parrot crying for silver coins.
sentences.zh: 有时我仍在梦里听到海浪声，还有鹦鹉索要银币的叫声。

picturePages.text: I have no wish to return to Treasure Island, because some things are worth more than gold.

sentences.en: I have no wish to return to Treasure Island, because some things are worth more than gold.
sentences.zh: 我不想再回金银岛，因为有些东西比黄金更有价值。

paragraphs: Treasure Island.
Chapter 1: The Sailor at the Inn. My name is Jim Hawkins, and this is the story of how I found treasure. My parents kept a small inn near the sea.
One day, an old sailor arrived with a heavy sea chest. He called himself the captain, but his real name was Billy Bones. He drank too much and sang loud songs about pirates.
He paid me to watch for a sailor with one leg. I began to see that man in my dreams. Billy frightened our guests, but Doctor Livesey was not afraid of him.
The doctor warned him that too much drink would kill him. Then a stranger called Black Dog came to the inn. He and Billy fought, and Black Dog ran away.
Billy fell ill, and I understood that his past had found him.
Chapter 2: The Map in the Chest. My father died while Billy was staying with us. My mother and I were grieving, and we needed money to keep the inn.
One evening, a blind man made me lead him to Billy. He put a small piece of paper into Billy's hand. It was the black spot, a warning from the pirates.
Billy tried to stand up, but he fell and died. Mother opened his chest to take the money he owed us. She refused to take more, even though we were in danger.
I took a packet of papers, and we escaped before the pirates arrived. Later, I showed the papers to the doctor and Squire Trelawney. Inside was a map showing where Captain Flint had buried his gold.
The squire promised to buy a ship, and suddenly my life became an adventure.
Chapter 3: A Friendly Man with One Leg. Our ship was called the Hispaniola. In Bristol, the squire hired a cook named Long John Silver.
Silver had one leg, a warm smile, and a parrot on his shoulder. His parrot shouted, "Pieces of eight!" I remembered Billy's warning, but Silver seemed too kind to be dangerous.
He told me about ships and treated me like a friend. He also helped the squire find sailors for our voyage. Captain Smollett did not like the way the voyage had been planned.

The squire had talked freely about the treasure, and everyone knew our secret. The captain moved the guns and powder to a safer place on the ship. I thought he was too strict, while Silver seemed wonderful.
I had not yet learned how easily a friendly face can hide a dangerous plan.
Chapter 4: Inside the Apple Barrel. One night, I climbed into a barrel to find an apple. Before I could climb out, Silver sat down beside it.
He began talking to two sailors, and I stayed very still. Silver had sailed with Captain Flint, and many of our sailors were pirates. They planned to let the captain find the treasure first.
Then they would take the ship and kill anyone who stood in their way. The man I trusted was quietly planning to destroy us. My heart beat hard, but I waited until the men had left.
I told the doctor, the squire, and the captain what I had heard. There were far more pirates than loyal men on board. We agreed to smile, keep our secret, and wait for a chance to act.
Now every friendly word from Silver made me feel cold.
Chapter 5: The Man in the Trees. When we reached the island, the captain let some sailors go ashore. I slipped into their boat because I wanted to see the island for myself.
Once we landed, I ran into the trees. I heard Silver arguing with Tom, an honest sailor. Tom refused to join the pirates, and Silver killed him.
I ran away in fear, no longer doubting what Silver could do. Then a thin man appeared among the trees and spoke my name. He was Ben Gunn, a sailor left on the island three years before.
He had survived alone, but he longed to go home and eat cheese again. Ben knew Silver, and he knew a great deal about Flint's treasure. He offered to help if the doctor would take him home.
Before we parted, he told me where he had hidden a little boat.
Chapter 6: The Wooden Fort. While I was exploring, the doctor and our loyal men left the ship. They carried food and guns to an old wooden fort with fresh water.
I found them there and told the doctor about Ben Gunn. The next morning, Silver arrived carrying a white flag. He offered to let us live if we gave him the treasure map.
Captain Smollett refused to trust a promise from a man who had betrayed us. Silver left in anger, and soon the pirates attacked. We fought from behind the wooden walls.
We held the fort, but several men died and the captain was badly hurt. The island no longer felt like a place for a wonderful adventure. People were paying for the treasure with their lives.
I wanted to help, but I was about to make another dangerous choice alone.
Chapter 7: A Small Boat at Night. The fort was hot, and I grew tired of waiting. Without asking anyone, I took some food and slipped away.
I found Ben Gunn's little boat beneath a white rock. It was light and round, and it was difficult to control. After dark, I pushed it into the sea and moved towards the Hispaniola.
Only two pirates were on the ship, and they were drinking and fighting. I cut the rope that held the ship in place. The ship began to drift, and I hoped the pirates would lose it.
But the sea also carried my small boat away from shore. Waves rose around me, and I could not make the boat obey. I was alone in the dark because I had refused to ask for help.
At last I fell asleep, too tired to fight the sea any longer.
Chapter 8: The Ship Is Mine. In the morning, I saw the Hispaniola drifting nearby. I managed to climb on board before my little boat sank.
One pirate was dead, and the other, Israel Hands, was badly hurt. I took down the pirate flag and said that the ship was mine. Hands offered to help me sail into the sheltered North Inlet.
I needed his knowledge, but I watched him carefully. While I was busy with the ship, he hid a knife. When we reached shallow water, he suddenly came after me.
I climbed up the mast, and he threw his knife into my shoulder. I fired my pistol, and Hands fell into the sea. Shaking with fear, I freed myself and covered the wound.
I had saved the ship, but I did not feel like a happy hero.
Chapter 9: Among the Pirates. That night, I walked back to the fort, hoping to find my friends. The place was dark, and I stepped inside quietly.
Suddenly, Silver's parrot cried out above my head. The pirates had taken the fort, and I was their prisoner. Silver told me that the doctor had given them the fort and the map.
I could not understand why my friends had done this. The pirates wanted to kill me, but Silver stood between us. He hoped I would speak for him if he ever faced a trial.
I told him that I had heard his plan and hidden the ship. His men grew angry and gave him another black spot. But Silver showed them the map and won back their trust.
He had protected me, yet I knew he was also protecting himself.
Chapter 10: A Promise to Keep. The next morning, Doctor Livesey came to treat the sick pirates. He helped them even though they were his enemies.
When he saw me, he looked both relieved and angry. I had left my friends without warning and put myself in danger. I told him that I was sorry and that the ship was safe in the North Inlet.
The doctor wanted me to run away with him. But I had promised Silver that I would not escape. I did not want to become a person whose words meant nothing.

The doctor listened, although it was hard for him to leave me there. He asked Silver to keep me safe and warned him to be careful at the treasure. The doctor seemed to know something that neither of us understood.
As he walked away, I hoped that keeping my promise was not a terrible mistake.
Chapter 11: The Empty Treasure Pit. Silver led the pirates into the forest, and I walked beside him. We found a skeleton with an arm pointing towards the treasure.
Flint had left it there as a sign, and the men were afraid. Then a strange voice rose from the trees, singing Flint's old song. Some pirates thought that a dead man had come back.
Silver kept them moving, but even he looked worried. At last we reached the place marked on the map. The treasure pit was empty, with only a few broken boards inside.
The pirates turned on Silver, believing that he had tricked them. Before they could attack us, shots came from the trees. The doctor, Ben Gunn, and our friend Gray rushed out and saved us.
Ben had found and moved the gold long before we arrived, and the strange voice was his.
Chapter 12: What We Took Home. Ben led us to his cave, where the gold lay in great piles. The doctor had learned his secret and given the pirates a useless map.
For days, we carried the heavy treasure to our ship. Silver worked hard beside us, always watching for his next chance. We left three surviving pirates on the island with food, tools, and medicine.

Then we sailed away from the place where so many people had died. At a port on our way home, Silver escaped with a bag of money. He had saved my life, but that did not erase the cruel things he had done.

We each received a share of the treasure, and I returned to my mother. The money made our lives easier, but it could not bring back the people we had lost. Sometimes I still hear the sea in my dreams and the parrot crying for silver coins.
I have no wish to return to Treasure Island, because some things are worth more than gold.

stories.title: A Tiny Seed
paragraphs: A Tiny Seed: The Story of Wangari Maathai Nicola Rijsdijk Maya Marshak English Level
In a village on the slopes of Mount Kenya in East Africa, a little girl worked in the fields with her mother. Her name was Wangari.
Wangari loved being outside. In her family’s food garden she broke up the soil with her machete. She pressed tiny seeds into the warm earth.

Her favourite time of day was just after sunset. When it got too dark to see the plants, Wangari knew it was time to go home. She would follow the narrow paths through the fields, crossing rivers as she went.

Wangari was a clever child and couldn’t wait to go to school. But her mother and father wanted her to stay and help them at home. When she was seven years old, her big brother persuaded her parents to let her go to school.

She liked to learn! Wangari learnt more and more with every book she read. She did so well at school that she was invited to study in the United States of America. Wangari was excited! She wanted to know more about the world.

At the American university Wangari learnt many new things. She studied plants and how they grow. And she remembered how she grew: playing games with her brothers in the shade of the trees in the beautiful Kenyan forests.
The more she learnt, the more she realised that she loved the people of Kenya. She wanted them to be happy and free. The more she learnt, the more she remembered her African home.

When she had finished her studies, she returned to Kenya. But her country had changed. Huge farms stretched across the land. Women had no wood to make cooking fires. The people were poor and the children were hungry.

Wangari knew what to do. She taught the women how to plant trees from seeds. The women sold the trees and used the money to look after their families. The women were very happy. Wangari had helped them to feel powerful and strong.
As time passed, the new trees grew into forests, and the rivers started flowing again. Wangari’s message spread across Africa. Today, millions of trees have grown from Wangari’s seeds.
Wangari had worked hard. People all over the world took notice, and gave her a famous prize. It is called the Nobel Peace Prize, and she was the first African woman ever to receive it.
Wangari died in 2011, but we can think of her every time we see a beautiful tree.
